papers.title: Opening the blackbox of LLM-based automated essay scoring: Insights into feature weighting patterns and score validity
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: LLM automated essay scoring feature weighting differs from human rubric priorities, raising score validity concerns.

papers.title: A framework for evaluation of large language models in essay assessment: Reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Framework evaluating LLM essay assessment for reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning.

papers.why: Fairness in K-12 predictions needs distribution checks, not averages.
papers.title: Beyond binary outcomes: Evaluating and mitigating bias in national standardized test score prediction
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Early schooling standardized test score predictions: balanced group representation did not guarantee fair predictions; proposes distribution-wide fairness metrics and data-specific debiasing.

papers.title: Optimizing automated scoring in ILSAs with prompt compression
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Prompt compression for automated scoring in international large-scale assessments.

papers.why: Early warning models miss life events; human outreach must check the story behind every flag.
papers.title: Predictive learning analytics in online education: A deeper understanding through explaining algorithmic errors
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Interviews with 27 online students whose at-risk predictions were wrong. Errors came from unforeseen life events: family and work changes, health, computer problems. Some new data sources could reduce errors.

papers.why: Warns districts not to trust a single vendor accuracy figure.
papers.title: Quantifying variability in predictions of student performance: Examining the impact of bootstrap resampling in data pipelines
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Bootstrapping showed student success predictions vary more than single accuracy numbers suggest; feature selection increased variability.

papers.why: Frames why assessment redesign is part of AI adoption, not just cheating prevention.
papers.title: Assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Position paper: traditional assessment is hard to design, gives snapshots, is not adapted to learners, fits school culture more than real-world culture, and tests skills humans now do with computers. Reviews AI approaches that partly address this and their new challenges.

papers.why: Shows districts can pool item banks for adaptive testing.
papers.title: The development and implementation of a computer adaptive progress test across European countries
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Consortium of 8 European medical schools built a shared computer adaptive progress test.

papers.title: Categorizing learning analytics models according to their goals and identifying their relevant components: A review of the learning analytics literature from 2011 to 2019
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Review of 101 articles sorts LA models into performance, meta-cognitive, interactivity, communication, and data models; 16 common components.

papers.why: Background for the early warning chapter.
papers.title: Four paradigms in learning analytics: Why paradigm convergence matters
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Position paper on learning analytics paradigms and the value of convergence with related fields.

papers.why: US K-12 early warning evidence on promise and bias risk.
papers.title: Using Machine Learning to Advance Early Warning Systems: Promise and Pitfalls
papers.venue: Teachers College Record: The Voice of Scholarship in Education
papers.finding: Machine learning can improve early warning indicators and create clear rules, but needs expertise, and black-box models invite users to read results through existing biases.

papers.title: Leveraging Parents through Low-Cost Technology
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, middle and high school: weekly automated texts on missed work, grades, and absences cut course failures 27% and raised class attendance 12%.

children.name: The Early Warning System
children.blurb: An early warning system tracks indicators that predict whether a student is falling off track, such as attendance, behavior incidents, and course performance, reviewed weekly or monthly.

children.name: Live Formative Checks
children.blurb: A live formative check is a quick question asked during a lesson, on a mini whiteboard or in a short online poll, that shows a teacher whether students understand before the class moves on.

children.name: Readiness Estimates
children.blurb: Readiness estimates are predictions drawn from benchmark results about which students are likely to pass state tests.

children.name: Benchmark and Item Analysis
children.blurb: Benchmark and item analysis is the practice of using periodic benchmark assessments and question level results to see how students are progressing and where instruction may need to change.

children.name: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
children.blurb: Growth data shows how much students have learned over time, while proficiency data shows where they stand against a standard, and both matter because a school with students starting far behind may show strong growth while proficiency stays low.

children.name: Reporting to Families
children.blurb: Reporting to Families is about giving families clear, timely information about their child's progress so they can help.

children.name: Student Self Assessment
children.blurb: Student self assessment is when students judge their own work against clear criteria and set their own goals for improvement, rather than waiting for a teacher or a tool to tell them what to fix.

children.name: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
children.blurb: This idea is that tests alone cannot show everything students know and can do, so schools should also use portfolios, performance tasks, and oral assessments.

children.name: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
children.blurb: AI has changed what some assessments can tell teachers, because a take home essay or problem set may now show what a tool can do rather than what a student can do.

children.name: Survey Analysis for School Improvement
children.blurb: Survey analysis for school improvement means using surveys of students, families, and staff to see experiences that test scores cannot show, then grouping open responses into themes with AI features in spreadsheet tools.

children.name: Building Data Skills in Staff
children.blurb: Building data skills in staff means training teachers and leaders to read assessment data well, including its uncertainty and its limits.

children.name: What Data Cannot Tell You
children.blurb: What Data Cannot Tell You is the idea that numbers from tests and attendance record only a slice of a student's learning and life.

children.name: Fairness Checks
children.blurb: Fairness checks are the practice of testing whether a data system's results treat groups of students fairly, rather than assuming fairness because the inputs look balanced.

children.name: Program Evaluation
children.blurb: Program evaluation is the practice of checking whether a program or tool actually works by comparing students who used it with similar students who did not.

children.name: Board and Accountability Reports
children.blurb: Board and accountability reports are documents that school leaders must produce for governing boards, campus improvement planning and state accountability submissions, and AI can help staff draft and organize them.

children.name: Protecting Student Data
children.blurb: Protecting student data means limiting what student information is collected, who can see it, and how long it is kept.

sections.body: This part of school life is how a school gathers and uses information about what students know and how they are doing, from early warning flags to benchmark tests, growth reports, portfolios, and reports to families and boards. The book describes AI here as a tool that can speed up analysis, spot patterns, and generate predictions, but it also warns that a single accuracy number can make predictions look more reliable than they are, and that the same prediction run on slightly different samples can flag different students. It treats assessment data, early warning flags, and predictions as things that can help teachers see who needs help and whether programs work, or can mislead, label, and harm when treated as certain. One privacy rule runs through the whole chapter: remove student names and identification numbers before analyzing data in any tool not covered by a signed data privacy agreement, while analysis inside the district's approved data systems can use identified data under proper access rules.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, as the book finds it, is data that leads to help: when a flag or a report is followed by outreach, and when fairness checks by group are run on flags and grades. What does not work is the dashboard nobody acts on, where a district buys a platform, builds impressive dashboards, and holds data meetings but no one follows up with the students the data identifies, or where hidden scores are read through staff assumptions. The rule the book holds to is that data starts conversations and never ends them, and that data collected but not used wastes time and money while data used to label rather than help causes harm. It also notes that most practices in this area are sound practices AI can make faster, with only one idea carrying strong evidence and one moderate, and it points to research on wrong at-risk predictions caused by unforeseen life events and on variability in predictions across resampling.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a chain from noticing to acting to checking. The Early Warning System and Live Formative Checks are where a teacher or leader goes to see who needs help now and how to follow up on every flag, while Readiness Estimates, Benchmark and Item Analysis, and Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency are where they go to understand what the data says about learning over time. Reporting to Families, Student Self Assessment, Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment, and Assessing Learning When Students Have AI are where a teacher or parent goes to see how learning is shown and shared, and Survey Analysis for School Improvement and Building Data Skills in Staff are where a leader goes to build the capacity to read and use data well. What Data Cannot Tell You, Fairness Checks, Program Evaluation, Board and Accountability Reports, and Protecting Student Data are where a leader or board member goes to test whether the data is fair, whether investments work, what the limits are, and whether privacy rules are being kept.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
